@@8008789 <h> Explained : The hurdles for Turnbull 's school funding plan <p> The public might think the flagged carve-up of school funding between the states and Commonwealth is unrealistic . In pure political terms it may well be . But in policy terms it 's worth considering , writes Jennifer Buckingham . <p> Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull has fanned the flames of the school funding debate yet again by revisiting the idea that responsibility for funding schools be carved up , with state government funding only state schools and the federal government funding only non-government schools . It is an idea worth exploring but it is not as simple as it sounds . <p> There are two major obstacles . One is that state schools rely on Commonwealth government funding because of the limited ability of state governments to raise revenue . It would only be fair and feasible to give state governments the full responsibility of funding schools if , as the Prime Minister has also suggested , the states can levy tax income for this purpose . <p> The second major obstacle is the Australian Education @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Commonwealth government must provide for schools , and would have to be superseded for the Commonwealth government to cease funding state schools . <p> While these roadblocks are substantial they are not insurmountable in theory . But there are a number of potential consequences - positive and negative , depending on one 's perspective - to be considered , and some questions to be answered . <p> One potential consequence is that if tax and spending on schools were more closely and clearly related , there would be greater taxpayer sensitivity and accountability for education quality . <p> At the moment , the states are able to blame any unwillingness on their part to increase school funding on the Commonwealth government holding the purse strings , as it controls both the size of the general grants given to states and the level of Commonwealth funding earmarked for schools . <p> Likewise , it would be more difficult for people who are against school choice to make the argument that non-government schools " take " funding from state schools , since their funding would come from different sources . <p> Without @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ over state schools . Again , this can be seen either as a pro or a con . <p> Funding levels for state schools would be determined by the states - and would not necessarily decrease as some doomsayers have predicted . <p> In the past , as well as providing general recurrent funding to state schools , the Commonwealth government funded numerous programs in schools , from financial literacy to travel subsidies for school students to visit Parliament House . These specific purpose funding programs have decreased in number in recent years but a couple of big funding levers remain - participation in NAPLAN and implementation of the national curriculum . Without the Commonwealth funding sweetener , participation of state school sectors in national initiatives like the national curriculum , NAPLAN and My School would be more difficult to secure . <p> However , before even getting to the point where these things might occur , there are some very practical policy questions to resolve . <p> Funding levels for state schools would be determined by the states - and would not necessarily decrease as some doomsayers have predicted . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ schools would be determined . <p> For the past couple of decades , non-government school funding has been indexed to state school funding . Currently , funding allocations for all schools start with the same basic formula - a student resource standard with additional weightings for school and student characteristics - with various exceptions and additions negotiated by the system or sector authorities . <p> This formula - called " Gonski " funding - has not yet been fully applied , and the Commonwealth government has not yet revealed its alternative funding model . A delineation of funding responsibilities along the lines proposed by the Prime Minister would not mean that the principles of the " Gonksi " model would be abandoned , but would require a new set of agreements . <p> Another question : If the Commonwealth government assumed full responsibility for funding non-government schools , would non-government schools still be registered and accredited by state government authorities ? At the moment , non-government schools are eligible for Commonwealth and state government funding only if they meet the registration standards set under state legislation and monitored by state authorities @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Standards . <p> Accreditation by the same authority is required for schools to offer education leading to qualifications such as the Higher School Certificate . It is not clear how changes in funding would affect changes in governance . <p> One of the criticisms of this proposal when it was first suggested last year was that it would lead to cost-shifting between levels of government ; the logic being that state governments would have an incentive to move students into the non-government sector to reduce the state education budget . This incentive already exists . State governments currently contribute much less to non-government schools than state schools . The proposed funding model may increase the cost-shifting incentive to some extent but it is not a new scenario . <p> Many commentators will be tempted to dismiss such a dramatic change in school funding arrangements as being unrealistic . In pure political terms , it may well be . But in policy terms it should be considered on its merits . <h> Ronald Ostrowski : <p> 01 Apr 2016 1:30:22pm <p> I wonder why the PM 's conversation does not extend to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ introduced . @@8011051 <p> The world must begin the shift to zero-carbon sources of electricity as soon as 2018 to avoid adding new fossil-fuel power plants that will lock in dangerous climate change , according to a team of Oxford University researchers . <p> Taking the average operating life of coal or gas-fired plants as 40 years , the world 's fleet of carbon-emitting power stations had already committed by 2014 a total of 87 per cent of the emissions required to ensure a 50-50 chance of reaching two degrees of warming compared with pre-industrial levels . <p> By 2017 , the remaining stock of potential emissions will have been locked in , necessitating a transition to renewable or zero-emissions electricity from then on . Alternatively , radical technologies will be needed to sequester carbon dioxide or extract it from the atmosphere , the researchers including Australian Cameron Hepburn wrote in a paper published in Applied Energy journal . <p> The window on curbing climate change is more narrow than many realise , a new study argues . Photo : Pat Scala <p> " For policymakers who think of climate change @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ wake-up call , " the authors said in a statement . " Whether we succeed or fail in containing warming to 2 degrees is being determined by actions we are taking right now . " <p> Electricity generation accounts for about one quarter of man-made greenhouse gas emissions and about one third of Australia 's total . The researchers assumed other emission sources , such as transport and agriculture , would track towards a 2-degree warming limit , an assumption " which may well be optimistic " , the paper notes . <p> Coal conundrum : shut down power plants early , but will emissions end up being higher ? Photo : Paul Jones <p> Australia was one of almost 200 nations to sign up to limiting warming to a 1.5-2 degree range at the Paris climate summit late last year . <p> The lower end of that target has been well exceeded , the researchers argue : " Meeting a 1.5-degree target without carbon capture and storage or asset stranding would have required all additions to the electricity sector were zero carbon from 2006 onwards , at the latest " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Climate &amp; Energy College , said the research confirmed work by the International Energy Agency and others " that we now have enough fossil fuel infrastructure globally in place to emit a detrimental amount of carbon " . <p> The Moree solar farm in NSW built by Fotowatio Renewable Ventures of Spain with Origin Energy taking its output from April 1 . Photo : Supplied <p> " With the correct market signals in place - such as a price on carbon emissions - it will be more economical even for the utilities to abandon fossil fuel plants and switch to renewable investments instead , " Associate Professor Meinshausen said . " If the time for halting investments into new fossil fuel infrastructure is 2017 for the world , that time has been 10 years ago for Australia - the highest per-capita emitter in the developed world . " <p> As it happens , the combination of Australia 's flat or declining demand for grid-supplied electricity and the need to meet the mandated 2020 Renewable Energy Target ( RET ) means there is little likelihood of new coal or gas-fired power plants @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ decade , said Dylan McConnell , a research fellow at Melbourne University 's Melbourne Energy Institute . <p> While there are several proposed gas projects and one black coal project in NSW at AGL 's Bayswater site , renewable energy ventures are likely to meet any near-term need for additional large-scale capacity , Mr McConnell said . <p> Some 14,000 megawatts ( MW ) of wind or solar plants are seeking approval , a tally that is " certainly much more than needed for the RET " , he said . " The cost curve for fossil fuel plants is going in the other direction . " <p> " Ten years ago , 15 years ago the prospectors were in Queensland looking for coal seam gas resources , " Grant King , Origin 's chief executive , said last year .
